title: ULD Types, Codes and Dimensions: A Forwarder’s Guide to Unit Load Devices
summary: ULD types, IATA codes and dimensions for forwarders: LD3, AKH, PMC and PAG. How ULD choice affects chargeable weight, BUP vs loose and booking.
body_markdown:
Your customer’s cargo stands 1.9 meters tall, and the airline wants to know which ULD you’re building – or whether the freight fits the lower deck at all.


A ULD, or[unit load device](https://www.freightos.com/glossary/what-is-a-unit-load-device/) , is the standardized aircraft container or pallet-and-net that airlines use to load cargo, identified by an IATA three-letter type code.


Below: a type table with ULD dimensions, how to read ULD codes, and what ULD choice changes in your quote and booking.

## **ULD Types at a Glance**


These are the ULD types you’ll quote most often, with typical values from published airline specs. Each airline sets its own limits by aircraft and position, so check before you commit to a build.


**Common name** **IATA type code** **Container or pallet** **Base size** **Height (contour)** **Indicative max gross weight** **Deck and typical aircraft**


LD3 AKE Container 156 x 153 cm (61.5 x 60.4 in) 163 cm (64 in) 1,588 kg (3,500 lb) Lower deck – A330, A350, A380, B777, B787


LD3-45 AKH Container 156 x 153 cm (61.5 x 60.4 in) 114 cm (45 in) 1,134 kg (2,500 lb) Lower deck – A320 family narrow-bodies


LD9 AAP Container 318 x 224 cm (125 x 88 in) about 160 cm (62–64 in) 4,625 kg (10,200 lb) lower deck Lower deck – most wide-bodies


PMC (P6P) PMC Pallet 318 x 244 cm (125 x 96 in) 163 cm lower deck; up to 300 cm (118 in) main deck 6,804 kg (15,000 lb) main deck; about 5,000–5,100 kg lower deck Lower and main deck – wide-bodies and freighters


PAG (P1P) PAG Pallet 318 x 224 cm (125 x 88 in) 163 cm lower deck; higher on main deck 6,804 kg (15,000 lb) main deck; 4,626 kg (10,200 lb) lower deck Lower and main deck – wide-bodies and freighters


Half pallet PLA Pallet 318 x 153 cm (125 x 60.4 in) 163 cm (64 in) 3,175 kg (7,000 lb) Lower deck – wide-bodies


M-1 AMA Container 318 x 244 cm (125 x 96 in) 244 cm (96 in) 6,804 kg (15,000 lb) Main deck – freighters (B747F, B777F, A330F)


## **ULD Containers vs Pallets: When Each Is Used**


ULD containers are enclosed units with walls, a roof and a door or curtain. Most are contoured to the curved lower hold of a wide-body.


Pallets are flat aluminum bases secured with a net and straps, and they’re the main-deck default on freighters.


- **Choose a container** for many small cartons, high-value goods or anything that shouldn’t be exposed to weather or pilferage.
- **Choose a pallet** for long, heavy or awkward pieces, or when you need main-deck height.


Certified ULDs carry an aviation authority airworthiness approval, usually under TSO-C90. Non-certified containers don’t, so they only fly where the aircraft’s weight and balance manual allows – rarely on a main deck. As[IATA](https://www.iata.org/en/programs/cargo/cargo-operations/unit-load-devices/) points out, ULDs are aircraft parts, subject to civil aviation rules on design, testing, repair and maintenance.


## **LD3 (AKE) Container: The Workhorse**


The LD3 container is the one most forwarders picture first. Its base is 156 x 153 cm, it stands 163 cm tall, and one side is contoured, so the top is wider (about 200 cm) than the base. Two sit side by side in the lower hold of wide-bodies from the A330 and A350 to the B777 and B787.


Published volume is about 4.3 CBM, tare is up to about 100 kg depending on the build, and max gross weight is 1,588 kg.


Nominal volume isn’t sellable volume, so don’t quote the brochure figure.


### **LD3-45 (AKH Container) for Narrow-Bodies**


The AKH container uses the same base as the AKE but stands only 114 cm (45 in) tall, so it fits the lower hold of A320-family aircraft. Volume drops to about 3.6 CBM. Cargo built into an AKE for the long-haul leg may need rebuilding, or to fly loose, on a narrow-body feeder sector.


## **ULD Pallets: PMC, PAG and Main-Deck Positions**


The PMC pallet, a standard main-deck and lower-deck pallet, has a base of 318 x 244 cm (125 x 96 in). In a wide-body lower deck it’s built to 163 cm; on a freighter’s main deck it can go to 244 cm or, in some positions, 300 cm (118 in).


The PAG pallet is narrower at 318 x 224 cm (125 x 88 in). Ask which one the carrier will release before you plan a build.


- **Net and straps:** a slack net or loose overhang gets the build rejected.
- **Contour:** a main-deck build is useless if the flight only has belly space.


## **How to Read a ULD Code**


ULD codes have three parts: a three-letter type code (category, base size, contour or restraint type), a serial number and a two-character owner code. AKE 12345 XX, for example, is a certified LD3-type container, serial 12345, owned by carrier XX.


**Position** **What it tells you** **Examples**


1st letter – category A = certified container; P = certified pallet; R = certified temperature-controlled container; D = non-certified container **A** KE, **P** MC, **R** KN


2nd letter – base size K = 156 x 153 cm; L = 318 x 153 cm; A = 318 x 224 cm; M = 318 x 244 cm A **K** E, P **L** A, P **A** G, P **M** C


3rd letter – contour or restraint Containers: shape and height profile; pallets: restraint type AK **E** (LD3), AK **H** (LD3-45), PM **C**


The serial number is four or five digits. The IATA-assigned owner code – usually an airline’s, sometimes a leasing company’s – tells you whose unit you’re holding and who will chase it if it’s late or damaged.


Type and contour codes are allocated under the IATA ULD Regulations (ULDR) .


## **ULD Dimensions, Contours and Aircraft Compatibility**


Base size decides whether a ULD locks into the floor; contour decides whether it fits the space above.


That’s why a unit accepted on one aircraft is refused on another. An AKE fits an A330 or B777 lower deck but not an A320. A PMC built to 300 cm needs a tall main-deck position on a freighter such as a B747F; on a passenger B787 it must be built to 163 cm.


Check every sector. Madrid–New York may be wide-body all the way; a Milan–Chicago routing with a narrow-body feeder leg changes which ULD the cargo can use.


## **How ULD Choice Affects Your Quote**


### **Loose Cargo vs Build-Up (BUP)**


Tender cargo is loose and the airline or its handler builds the ULD. Deliver a build-up (BUP) unit and your warehouse or handling agent loads, nets and weighs it to the airline’s rules, ready for carriage.


BUP can save handling time and unlock ULD rates, but it moves risk to you: the build must meet contour and weight limits, and the unit must come back on time and intact. Late returns can trigger demurrage, and damage can be billed to whoever held the unit.


### **Chargeable Weight, ULD Rates and Pivot Weight**


Loose cargo is rated on chargeable weight: the higher of actual and volumetric weight. Use a[chargeable weight calculator](https://www.freightos.com/freight-resources/chargeable-and-volumetric-weight-calculator-freightos/) to check it fast.


BUP freight is often rated differently. Many airlines charge a ULD rate up to a set “pivot weight” for that ULD type, then an over-pivot rate per kg above it. Pivot weights and any tare deduction vary by airline, route and ULD type, so check the carrier’s tariff.


Illustrative example (weights only, fictional pivot weight):


**Loose** **BUP on one lower-deck PMC**


Actual weight 1,100 kg 1,100 kg


Volume 9.6 CBM 9.6 CBM


Volumetric weight (6,000 cm³/kg) 1,600 kg not used


Billed weight 1,600 kg chargeable 1,500 kg pivot (cargo is below pivot)


Low-density cargo often rates better built up, because volume stops driving the bill. Small or dense loads can go the other way, paying a pivot they never fill. And 9.6 CBM is close to the roughly 10.9 CBM envelope of a belly PMC, so confirm the build plan first.


### **Contour and Height Limits That Kill a Quote**


Before the rate goes to your customer, check:


1. **Piece height** for every sector – 163 cm in most lower decks, 114 cm in an AKH.
2. **Gross weight per position** , including tare.
3. **Floor-loading limits** for heavy, small-footprint pieces.
4. **Special handling** – dangerous goods or pharma may need a specific ULD type.

## **Booking ULD Capacity With Airlines**


1. **Confirm aircraft type and deck** for every sector.
2. **Confirm ULD type and availability** at origin, especially PMCs at peak.
3. **Agree release and return times** , with a signed ULD Control Receipt (UCR) at every handover.
4. **Agree BUP or loose** and who builds.
5. **Get ULD charges up front** – build-up, demurrage, damage – before they eat the margin.
6. **Check your booking route.** With[IATA accreditation](https://www.freightos.com/freight-resources/iata-freight-forwarders-accreditation-cargo-bookings/) you book airlines directly; non-IATA forwarders need another route.

## **Damaged or Unserviceable ULDs: What It Means for You**


A ULD damaged beyond allowable limits – a bent base, torn net or broken door – is unserviceable.


Under IATA guidance, it’s tagged and taken out of service, and the cargo moves to a serviceable unit . For you, that can mean a rebuild, a missed flight and, if the unit was in your custody, a damage charge. IATA estimates the annual cost of ULD repair and loss at $330 million . Inspect each unit on release, note damage on the UCR and photograph it.

## **The Bottom Line**


ULDs in air cargo come down to three checks: type code, base size and contour for every sector. Rate the cargo loose and built up, and agree ULD charges before you confirm. When a built unit wins, book it online with participating airlines in Freightos for Forwarders.


## Frequently Asked Questions


What Does ULD Stand for in Aviation?


ULD stands for unit load device. It’s an aircraft container, or a pallet secured with a net, that groups cargo, baggage or mail into one unit that locks into the aircraft’s cargo restraint system. Each ULD carries an IATA type code that identifies its category, base size and contour or restraint type.


What Is the 3-Letter Code on a ULD?


The three letters are the IATA type code. The first gives the category (for example, A for a certified container or P for a certified pallet), the second gives the base size, and the third gives the contour (for pallets, the restraint type). AKE is the LD3 container, PMC a 318 x 244 cm pallet, and AKH the narrow-body LD3-45.


What Are the Consequences of Using a Non-Serviceable ULD?


A ULD damaged beyond allowable limits can’t restrain its load as designed, which is a flight-safety risk. In practice, the unit is tagged and taken out of service, the cargo is moved to a serviceable ULD and may miss its flight, and the party holding the unit may face repair or damage charges.


What Is the Difference Between a ULD and a Shipping Container?


A ULD is a lightweight aircraft unit, usually aluminum or composite, shaped to fit an aircraft hold and locked into its floor. An ocean shipping container is a heavy steel box built to ISO standards for ships, trucks and rail. They aren’t interchangeable, and ULDs are much smaller.
